summary: Merge two sorted linked lists into one sorted list by splicing their nodes.
mainInsight: Walk both lists with one pointer each, always attaching the smaller head to the tail of the result; a dummy head removes the empty-result special case and the remaining tail is attached in one step.

approaches.name: Recursion
approaches.summary: merge(l1, l2) picks the smaller head and recurses on the rest.

approaches.name: Iterative with a dummy head
approaches.summary: Splice nodes while both lists are non-empty; attach the leftover list.

cards.answer: Two pointers with a dummy head: always attach the smaller of the two current heads, then the leftover list. Clue: Both lists are already sorted and have to be merged by splicing their nodes, so repeatedly attach the smaller of the two current heads.
keyPoints: Both lists are already sorted and have to be merged by splicing their nodes, so repeatedly attach the smaller of the two current heads.
cards.explanation: Sorted inputs mean the next output node is always one of the two heads, so a pointer per list and a dummy head finish it in one pass.

promptVariants: What does the dummy head simplify when merging lists?

options: It removes the special case for the first result node
It sorts the nodes of both lists as they are merged
It stores the length of the merged list so far
It reverses the lists before they are merged together
cards.answer: It removes the special case for the first result node
cards.explanation: The tail pointer always has a node to attach to; the answer is dummy.next.

promptVariants: Why can the leftover list be attached in one assignment?
What happens when one list is exhausted?
cards.answer: Both inputs are sorted, so once one list is empty the remaining nodes of the other are already in order and all >= everything placed so far. Pointing the tail at the remainder finishes the merge without copying.
cards.explanation: Splicing nodes (not copying values) keeps O(1) extra space.

cards.explanation: Only a dummy node and pointers; nodes are reused.

promptVariants: Why `if list1.val > list2.val` picks list2 and is that stable for equal values?
What does `p = p.next` do each iteration?
cards.answer: list2 is taken only when its value is strictly smaller; on ties list1 goes first, so equal elements keep their original relative order (stable). p always moves to the node just attached, so it is the tail of the merged list.
cards.explanation: Same as the merge step of merge sort.

promptVariants: What is returned when one list is empty?

cards.explanation: The loop is skipped and the leftover list is attached to the dummy (both empty returns None).
